title: She proposed
hookLine: Khadijah, respected and independent, proposes marriage through a friend

lines: A MESSAGE FROM A MERCHANT'S HOUSE.
TO A MAN WITH NO FORTUNE.
cards: A message leaves a merchant's house in Mecca, carried quietly by a friend. It comes from a woman of standing, with her own wealth and her own trade. It goes to a young man with no fortune at all.
She has heard Maysarah's report about the man who led her caravan, weighed it, and made up her mind. The friend's question sounds casual: what's keeping him from marriage? It isn't casual at all.

teach.b: Khadijah wasn't marrying for money; she had her own goods on the road and men hired to trade them. What she was choosing was a person.

In Ibn Ishaq's telling, she sends word to him with her reasons: the family tie between them, his good name among his people, his trustworthiness, his character, his truthfulness. Not his money; he had little.
Another report, in Ibn Sa'd, says she first sent a friend, a woman named Nafisa, to ask him quietly what was keeping him from marriage. He said he had nothing to marry with.
And Nafisa asked: and if that were taken care of, and you were invited by beauty, wealth, standing and a good match? So the go-between opened the door, and Khadijah walked through it.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told his uncles, the families met, and the marriage was made. The sources give different names for who spoke for her family; they agree on who asked first.

Much later, the Qur'an describes what a marriage is meant to hold. In Pickthall's words: "He ordained between you love and mercy." And a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari answers her choice from the other side.
Years on, the angel Jibril comes to the Prophet and says: Khadijah is on her way to you with a dish of food.
When she arrives, give her greetings of peace from her Lord, and from me.
A woman who chose, and was greeted by name.

how: Muslims remember Khadijah as Umm al-Mu'minin, a mother of the believers, and her proposal is often retold in talks on marriage and on the dignity of women in the Prophet's ﷺ life.

o: he asked Khadijah to marry him after the caravan
his uncles arranged a match with a rich widow
Khadijah asked him to marry her, for his character

p: the friend who asked him first
brought her greetings from her Lord

s: Ibn Ishaq describes her as already wealthy; her reasons were his trustworthiness and character.
a friend asked him first what kept him from marriage
Ibn Sa'd's report names her friend Nafisa.
in a hadith, Khadijah is greeted by her Lord
Jibril tells the Prophet to give her greetings from her Lord, in Sahih al-Bukhari.

games.q: Nafisa asks him why he hasn't married. he has almost nothing to offer. what does he say?
o: that he has no wish to marry.
that he has nothing to marry with.
that his uncles must choose for him.
games.why: he says he has nothing to marry with, so Nafisa asks: and if that were taken care of? the door was opened by a woman, for a woman.

practice: Bring to mind a woman who made a decision others wouldn't have made, and stood behind it: a grandmother, a boss, a teacher, a friend. Name, quietly and specifically, the reasons you trust her, the way Khadijah named hers.
If you pray, ask good for her by name; if not, hold her in mind with gratitude.

wordCard.voice: She proposed. Khadijah, a merchant of standing, asked the Prophet to marry her, through a friend and with her own reasons, for the sake of his character. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a proposal of marriage, the asking.

carryVoice: Your line: she chose him. Her reasons were about who he was. Day seven hundred seventeen, done.

sources.q: He ordained between you love and mercy.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (Khadijah as a merchant woman of dignity and wealth; her proposal and her reasons; his uncles)
Ibn Sa'd, Kitab al-Tabaqat al-Kabir (Nafisa bint Munya as go-between)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3820 (Jibril: give Khadijah greetings from her Lord and from me)
